sections.description: First steps in asking questions, noticing and sorting, kind teamwork and sharing your ideas from Stage 1.

remediation.title: What do we know about jobs?

questions.question: Halima wants to find out where the rice in her kitchen comes from. What should she do first?
questions.options: Hide the packet away | Read the packet label to see what it says | Wait for someone to tell her one day | Guess and tell the class her guess
questions.correctAnswer: Read the packet label to see what it says
questions.explanation: The label on a food packet is a source of information — it can tell Halima where the rice comes from. Good finders-out start by looking at what is right in front of them.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: Where does food come from?

questions.question: A farmer is visiting the class to talk about food. Which question would help the children find out the most?
questions.options: Do you like your farm? | Where does your milk go after it leaves the farm? | Can we go out to play now? | Is milk white?
questions.correctAnswer: Where does your milk go after it leaves the farm?
questions.explanation: A big open question lets the farmer explain the whole food journey. Yes-or-no questions only get very short answers.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: Where does food come from?

questions.question: Which of these sentences is an opinion, not a fact?
questions.options: Milk comes from cows | Bananas grow on plants | Rice needs water to grow | Mangoes are the most delicious fruit of all
questions.correctAnswer: Mangoes are the most delicious fruit of all
questions.explanation: ‘Most delicious’ tells us what someone likes, and different people like different things — that makes it an opinion. The other sentences can be checked and shown to be true.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: Where does food come from?

questions.question: The class is making a display about the journey of bread. What would make the display easiest for visitors to understand?
questions.options: One picture with nothing written at all | Lots of tiny writing with no pictures | Pictures mixed up in any order | Pictures in order with a clear label under each one
questions.correctAnswer: Pictures in order with a clear label under each one
questions.explanation: A display shares what you learned with other people. Pictures in the right order with clear labels let visitors follow the bread’s journey step by step.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: Where does food come from?

questions.question: Ayan washes an empty jam jar and uses it as a pencil pot. Which of the three Rs is she using?
questions.options: Repair | Recycle | Reduce | Reuse
questions.correctAnswer: Reuse
questions.explanation: Ayan is using the jar again for a new job instead of throwing it away. Using something again is called reusing.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What happens if we waste things?

questions.question: The class counts the rubbish in the playground and makes a tally chart. What can the tally chart tell them?
questions.options: What the weather will be tomorrow | Who dropped each piece of rubbish | Which class is best at football | Which kind of rubbish was found most often
questions.correctAnswer: Which kind of rubbish was found most often
questions.explanation: A tally chart records how many of each kind you counted. Comparing the tallies shows which kind of rubbish turned up most often.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What happens if we waste things?

questions.question: Sahra wants to find out how litter can hurt sea animals. Which source would help her most?
questions.options: A storybook about a talking fish | Guessing an answer quickly | A funny cartoon about pirates | A library book about sea animals
questions.correctAnswer: A library book about sea animals
questions.explanation: A book about real sea animals gives true information. Storybooks and cartoons are fun, but they are made up — and guessing is not finding out.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What happens if we waste things?

questions.question: The class is making an anti-waste poster. Which words would work best on it?
questions.options: A very long story in very small writing | Reduce, reuse, recycle — keep our beach clean! | No words and no pictures at all | Words in a secret code only the class knows
questions.correctAnswer: Reduce, reuse, recycle — keep our beach clean!
questions.explanation: A poster needs a short, clear message that people can read quickly and remember. Long stories and secret codes are hard for passers-by to understand.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What happens if we waste things?

questions.question: The class survey shows that plastic bottles are the most common waste at school. Which idea makes the best use of what they found out?
questions.options: Put a bottle-collecting bin in the playground | Paint the school gate a new colour | Ask everyone to talk more quietly | Buy more plastic bottles
questions.correctAnswer: Put a bottle-collecting bin in the playground
questions.explanation: The survey showed the real problem was plastic bottles, so the best idea is one that helps with bottles. Good ideas grow out of what you found.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What happens if we waste things?

questions.question: Bilal wants to know which game his classmates like best. What should he do?
questions.options: Ask each classmate and write down their answers | Look out of the window and wait | Choose his own favourite for everyone | Ask only his best friend
questions.correctAnswer: Ask each classmate and write down their answers
questions.explanation: A survey means asking everyone and recording the answers. Asking one friend or guessing would not show what the whole class thinks.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: How can we be active and healthy?

questions.question: In the class survey, 10 children chose football, 6 chose skipping and 2 chose swimming. What do the results show?
questions.options: Every child chose the same game | Swimming was the most popular game | Football was the most popular game | Nobody likes playing games
questions.correctAnswer: Football was the most popular game
questions.explanation: 10 is more than 6 and more than 2, so more children chose football than anything else. Reading the numbers carefully shows what a survey found.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: How can we be active and healthy?

questions.question: Hodan tried a new skipping game and kept getting tangled in the rope. What is the most helpful thing for her to think?
questions.options: I will never try anything new again | It is the rope’s fault, so I give up | What could I change to do better next time? | Nobody should ever play skipping games
questions.correctAnswer: What could I change to do better next time?
questions.explanation: Thinking about what happened and what to change is called reflection. It helps us get better — much more than blaming the rope!
questions.sourceUnitTitle: How can we be active and healthy?

questions.question: The class is planning a healthy-living stall. Bilal and Nimo both want to be the person who welcomes visitors. What should they do?
questions.options: Talk about it and agree to take turns | Stop helping with the stall at all | Both shout until one gives up | Let nobody welcome the visitors
questions.correctAnswer: Talk about it and agree to take turns
questions.explanation: Teams work best when people talk kindly and share the jobs. Taking turns means both friends get to help and the stall still runs well.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: How can we be active and healthy?

questions.question: Zahra wants to know what it feels like to move to a new town. What is the best way to find out?
questions.options: Ask someone who has never moved anywhere | Make up an answer that sounds exciting | Ask someone who has really moved to tell her about it | Copy a friend’s guess
questions.correctAnswer: Ask someone who has really moved to tell her about it
questions.explanation: The best information comes from people who have really lived it. Interviewing someone who moved gives Zahra true answers, not guesses.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What is it like to move here?

questions.question: Yusuf wrote: ‘When I first moved here I felt lonely, but a kind boy showed me where to play, and now I feel at home.’ What changed how Yusuf felt?
questions.options: He got a new school bag | Nothing changed for Yusuf | The weather became sunnier | A kind boy helped him find a place to play
questions.correctAnswer: A kind boy helped him find a place to play
questions.explanation: Reading carefully shows the change: Yusuf felt lonely, then a kind boy helped him, and after that he felt at home. Finding the reason inside a text is careful analysis.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What is it like to move here?

questions.question: A new child who has just moved here joins the class and knows nobody. What is the kindest thing to do?
questions.options: Ignore them until they go away | Invite them to join your game and learn their name | Laugh because they do not know the rules | Tell them all the seats are taken
questions.correctAnswer: Invite them to join your game and learn their name
questions.explanation: Welcoming a new person helps them feel happy, safe and like they belong. Kind actions make our class a team everyone can join.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What is it like to move here?

questions.question: Yusuf is writing an advice letter to a child who is about to move to a new town. What should he put in the letter?
questions.options: Words meant to make the child feel scared | A list of his ten favourite dinners | Helpful ideas, like how to make new friends | Nothing, so the letter stays empty
questions.correctAnswer: Helpful ideas, like how to make new friends
questions.explanation: An advice letter is for helping the reader. Clear, kind, useful ideas — like how to make friends — are exactly what a child who is moving needs.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What is it like to move here?

questions.question: Amina wants to know what games her grandmother played as a little girl. What should Amina do?
questions.options: Say nothing and forget the question | Ask her grandmother and listen to her answer | Ask her baby brother instead | Guess and never check
questions.correctAnswer: Ask her grandmother and listen to her answer
questions.explanation: Grandmother is the person who really knows! Asking the right person and listening carefully is how we find things out.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What can families teach us?

questions.question: Khadija’s grandfather taught her how to plant a seed. What is a lovely thing for Khadija to do?
questions.options: Hide the seeds so no one can plant them | Say thank you and tell him what she learned | Say the seed planted itself | Walk away without a word
questions.correctAnswer: Say thank you and tell him what she learned
questions.explanation: Saying thank you and talking about what you learned shows you noticed the help you were given. That is thankful thinking!
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What can families teach us?

questions.question: Libaan is telling the class about his family. What will help the class understand him best?
questions.options: Showing his family drawing and speaking clearly | Whispering with his back to the class | Holding his drawing upside down and saying nothing | Talking about something completely different
questions.correctAnswer: Showing his family drawing and speaking clearly
questions.explanation: When we share, a clear voice and a picture to point at help everyone follow along. Show and tell works best when we do both!
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What can families teach us?

questions.question: The class must choose one garden to draw together, but everyone likes a different garden. What is the fairest thing to do?
questions.options: Let the loudest child decide alone | Draw nothing and argue all day | Pick a garden without telling anyone | Listen to everyone’s idea and then vote
questions.correctAnswer: Listen to everyone’s idea and then vote
questions.explanation: In a team, every voice matters. Listening first and voting together is a fair way to choose when friends want different things.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What kind of garden would be best?

questions.question: Warsan is sorting picture cards into ‘things a plant needs’ and ‘things a plant does not need’. Which card goes in the ‘needs’ group?
questions.options: A pair of shoes | A television | A pillow | Water
questions.correctAnswer: Water
questions.explanation: Plants need water, light and soil to grow. Sorting things into the right groups helps us see what really matters.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What kind of garden would be best?

questions.question: Hassan is asking his aunt about her job as a nurse. Which question would find out the most?
questions.options: What do you do at work each day? | Do you have a job, yes or no? | What colour is my school bag? | Is your job a job?
questions.correctAnswer: What do you do at work each day?
questions.explanation: Open questions that start with ‘what’ invite long, interesting answers. Yes-or-no questions stop after one word.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What do we know about jobs?

questions.question: Sagal says, ‘Only boys can be doctors.’ What is the best reply?
questions.options: Doctors are not real | Nobody can be a doctor | Girls and boys can both be doctors | You are right, only boys can
questions.correctAnswer: Girls and boys can both be doctors
questions.explanation: When we hear an idea, we can stop and ask: is that really true? Girls and boys can do any job, so the fair and true reply is that both can be doctors.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What do we know about jobs?

questions.question: Ayaan is choosing the job she would like when she grows up. What is the best way to choose?
questions.options: Pick whatever her friend picked without thinking | Choose the first word she hears | Think about what she enjoys and is good at | Refuse to think about it
questions.correctAnswer: Think about what she enjoys and is good at
questions.explanation: Thinking about yourself — what you love and what you do well — is reflection. It helps you make choices that are right for you.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What do we know about jobs?

questions.question: Which of these actions saves water?
questions.options: Watering the path instead of the plants | Filling the bath and forgetting about it | Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth | Leaving the tap running all day
questions.correctAnswer: Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth
questions.explanation: Water is precious. Sorting actions into ‘save’ and ‘waste’ shows us that turning off the tap keeps clean water from running away.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: How can we save water?

questions.question: Omar thinks the leaking tap at school wastes a lot of water. What should he do to find out?
questions.options: Say it wastes a million buckets without checking | Shut his eyes and hope it stops | Walk past and never look at it | Watch the tap and count the drips
questions.correctAnswer: Watch the tap and count the drips
questions.explanation: Counting the drips is collecting real evidence. Then Omar can show everyone how much water is lost, instead of just guessing.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: How can we save water?

questions.question: Fatima drew a picture to teach others how to save water. What makes her picture really helpful?
questions.options: It is scribbles no one can understand | It is hidden inside her desk | It clearly shows someone turning off a tap | It shows her favourite cartoon instead
questions.correctAnswer: It clearly shows someone turning off a tap
questions.explanation: A picture can share an idea without any words — but only if people can see what it shows. Clear pictures teach; hidden scribbles cannot.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: How can we save water?
